paragraphs: This paper treats connected handwriting as a problem of planning and controlling continuous movement. Its central proposal is that a trajectory should minimize changes in torque, the turning forces that drive movement. This gives the model a physical optimization principle for producing a written path, implemented through a forward-inverse-relaxation neural network.

The intended character is represented through via-points: locations that the movement must pass through. These impose hard constraints while leaving the rest of the trajectory to the optimization process. The paper also proposes a way to estimate these points by repeatedly generating a character trajectory and extracting via-points from the resulting character.

The generated trajectories show good quantitative agreement with human handwriting data. The authors then use movement generation as the basis for a recognition scheme and demonstrate its application to handwritten characters. They also propose extending this approach to estimating phoneme timing in natural speech, connecting recognition with a model of how continuous actions are produced.
neurips-1993-a-computational-model-for-c.tldr: A handwriting model generates human-like trajectories by minimizing torque changes while passing through estimated character-defining points.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether a small, fixed neural network can learn nearly as well as the same network with optimal weights, given sufficiently long training. The distinction matters because earlier negative learning results considered what happens as the number of network nodes grows without bound. That setting does not directly answer the authors’ fixed-network question.

The analysis uses an agnostic refinement of probably approximately correct learning. Here, the learning target need not satisfy a predetermined structural assumption, training data may contain noise, and inputs and outputs can take non-Boolean values. Success therefore means approaching the best true error available within the chosen network, rather than necessarily eliminating error.

The authors give a positive answer in this framework and obtain a positive result for multilayer networks in the original PAC model as a special case. They also describe an efficient parallel implementation of their algorithm. The contribution is a learnability guarantee framed around prolonged training of a fixed analog network.
neurips-1993-agnostic-pac-learning-of-fu.tldr: For small fixed analog networks, the paper establishes learning guarantees that approach optimal-weight performance despite noise and unrestricted targets.

paragraphs: This paper describes a physical electronic model of saccadic eye movements, the rapid movements used to redirect gaze. It belongs to a broader effort to understand the primate eye-movement system and its relationship to visual attention. The researchers use analog CMOS VLSI technology to build a compact, low-power system that responds to real visual inputs in real time.

The reported early version links several specialized components. A one-dimensional photoreceptor array represents the retina. Another circuit computes the mean location of activity, representing a function of the superior colliculus. A saccadic burst generator supplies the movement-related signal, and a rotational platform models the mechanical dynamics of the eye-movement apparatus.

These components bring sensing, location computation, movement generation, and physical motion into one working system. Its scope is explicitly limited to a one-dimensional sensor and a platform with one rotational degree of freedom. Within that scope, the implementation provides a concrete way to study how proposed biological functions interact during visually driven movement.
neurips-1993-an-analog-vlsi-saccadic-eye.tldr: A compact analog chip system models visually driven eye movements through linked sensing, neural computation, and mechanical motion.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a method for choosing a layered neural-network model and its parameters within the same optimization process. Those are connected decisions: the model determines the form of the network being fitted, while its parameter values determine the behavior of that particular model. The authors seek a practical procedure that handles both together.

The method begins with a conventional information criterion and modifies it into a differentiable function of the parameters. Differentiability makes the modified criterion accessible to optimization through its local changes. The procedure then minimizes this function while progressively controlling it back toward the ordinary form of the criterion.

The key idea is to make the selection objective easier to optimize without abandoning the original criterion as the intended destination. This connects the computational convenience of a modified objective with the model-selection role of the conventional one. The authors discuss the method’s effectiveness through both theoretical analysis and experiments, presenting it as a joint approach to model and parameter optimization.
neurips-1993-an-optimization-method-of-l.tldr: A differentiable modification of an information criterion allows neural-network model selection and parameter fitting to proceed together.

paragraphs: An autoencoder converts an input into a code and then reconstructs the input from that code. This paper derives a training objective from minimum description length: minimize the information needed to describe both the code and whatever reconstruction error remains. This links representation learning to the combined cost of storing a representation and explaining its inaccuracies.

The authors show that the information cost is minimized by selecting codes stochastically from a Boltzmann distribution. The generative weights determine the energy assigned to each possible code for a given input. For distributed representations, however, evaluating this distribution requires considering exponentially many possible codes, making the exact solution computationally expensive.

The recognition weights provide an approximation to that distribution and yield an upper bound on description length. Even a loose bound can serve as a Lyapunov function, providing an objective that guides learning of both recognition and generative weights. The authors demonstrate learning factorial codes, showing how the approximate objective supports useful representation learning despite the cost of exact code selection.
neurips-1993-autoencoders-minimum-descri.tldr: The paper trains autoencoders through a tractable upper bound on the information needed to encode inputs and reconstruction errors.

paragraphs: This paper studies how many recurrent-network nodes are needed to implement a finite-state machine with m states. A finite-state machine maintains a state and changes it as inputs arrive; a recurrent network offers another way to realize that behavior. The central question is how efficiently the network can represent and carry out the machine’s operation.

The analysis compares unrestricted networks with two constrained forms. In one, weights and thresholds must take values from the set containing minus one and plus one. In the other, each node can receive only two inputs. The authors establish upper bounds on node requirements for these settings, including a bound linear in m for the two-input restriction.

They also provide matching lower bounds under an explicit assumption: the machine’s state can be encoded in a subset of nodes whose size grows logarithmically with m. Matching bounds identify the required scaling under that assumption. The results connect implementation efficiency to both the permitted network components and the way machine states are represented.
neurips-1993-bounds-on-the-complexity-of.tldr: The paper bounds the nodes needed to implement finite-state machines in recurrent networks under different architectural restrictions.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether an artificial neural network can classify electroencephalogram signals from different subject groups. The groups include normal subjects and subjects with psychiatric disorders, with obsessive compulsive disorder and schizophrenia given as examples. The task is to assign EEG signals to the relevant categories using patterns present in the recordings.

The chosen model is a multilayer perceptron. In this application, the network provides the connection between the EEG input and the classification decision. The research question concerns whether this class of network can learn distinctions that remain useful when it encounters signals outside the examples used to train it.

The authors report that the network classifies previously unseen test EEG signals with high accuracy. The use of unseen signals is central to the finding: the reported capability extends beyond handling the training examples themselves. The result supports multilayer perceptrons as an approach to this EEG classification problem, with the stated evidence focused on distinguishing the subject groups through their recorded signals.
neurips-1993-classification-of-electroen.tldr: A multilayer perceptron reportedly classifies unseen EEG signals from normal subjects and subjects with psychiatric disorders with high accuracy.

paragraphs: The paper introduces the Binary Diamond, a feed-forward neural network intended for classification. Its distinctive features are one-shot learning from examples and the ability to recruit additional neurons as needed. Learning and network growth are therefore connected parts of the proposed design, rather than requiring the entire network size to be settled in advance.

The approach is motivated by classification through clues. An item has basic features, and a clue can be any combination of those features. Such combinations are associated both with the items that contain them and with classes stored in memory. This gives the design a way to frame classification in terms of feature combinations that support particular category assignments.

The network is demonstrated and evaluated on pixel classification, where the authors report good performance. They also outline possible uses in associative memory. The contribution combines a proposed general-purpose classifier with a concrete application, emphasizing how examples, feature combinations, and the recruitment of neurons can work together in a classification system.
neurips-1993-classification-of-multi-spe.tldr: The Binary Diamond network combines one-shot learning and neuron recruitment for classification, with a successful pixel-classification demonstration.

paragraphs: Airlines prepare crew schedules in advance, but delays and absent crew members can force those schedules to change. This paper frames the resulting rescheduling decision as a best-choice problem: select the best available solution from a set of candidates without needing to establish a complete ranking of every candidate.

The authors adapt a neural-network comparison paradigm previously applied to backgammon. The connection is the structure of the decision, since both settings require choosing among possible alternatives. They explain the architecture and learning strategy of a backpropagation network mathematically, focusing on how it can support this kind of selection rather than a full ordering.

The paper also describes how to accelerate the network’s learning phase and applies the model to real crew-rescheduling problems from Sabena. This application gives the comparison approach an operational setting beyond game decisions. Its significance is the formulation of rescheduling around the choice that must actually be made, and a learning method organized around that requirement.
neurips-1993-comparison-training-for-a-r.tldr: A comparison-trained neural network selects among airline crew-rescheduling options without requiring a complete ranking.

paragraphs: This paper examines how prediction error on new examples changes as a multilayer network receives more training data. It studies a fully connected committee machine using statistical mechanics, calculating average generalization error through the replica formalism. The analysis applies in the limit where the number of hidden units becomes large.

The findings depend on how the training-set size scales with the network. When the number of examples is proportional to the number of inputs, the generalization error approaches a finite value. When the number of examples is proportional to the number of weights, the analysis instead reveals abrupt downward jumps in error as the training-set size changes.

These jumps are described as first-order phase transitions and occur for both binary and continuous weights. The result shows that improvement with additional examples can be discontinuous in this theoretical setting. It also makes the scaling choice consequential: relating data quantity to input size leads to different behavior from relating it to the number of adjustable weights.
neurips-1993-discontinuous-generalizatio.tldr: Large committee machines can show abrupt drops in generalization error when training data scales with the number of weights.

paragraphs: The binding problem asks how separate visual features become grouped into coherent perceived objects. This paper proposes that binding and segmentation depend on two complementary mechanisms. One uses spatial organization at low resolution and is described as resource-free; the other uses timing at high resolution and has limited resources.

The spatial mechanism depends on the orderly topographic arrangement of visual cortical areas. The temporal mechanism is proposed as potentially related to observed timing relationships between neuronal activities. Together, they offer different ways to associate features, with the high-resolution process carrying an explicit capacity limitation that the low-resolution process does not share.

Computer simulations illustrate how the two mechanisms could contribute to separating figures from backgrounds, inferring depth from occlusion, and determining the vividness of perceptual completion. These examples connect the proposed mechanisms to the construction of intermediate visual representations. The contribution is a computational account in which spatial organization and temporal coordination play complementary roles in turning fragmented visual information into perceived objects.
neurips-1993-dual-mechanisms-for-neural-.tldr: A proposed visual-binding model combines low-resolution spatial grouping with a resource-limited, high-resolution temporal mechanism.

paragraphs: This paper explains why a neural circuit’s behavior depends on the chemical environment in which it operates. Biological neurons possess many voltage-dependent currents, and the balance among these currents helps determine each neuron’s intrinsic activity. A neuron’s contribution to a circuit therefore depends on its own electrical properties as well as its connections.

Neuromodulatory substances can change that balance of conductances and also alter synaptic strength. These provide two routes for changing network behavior: modifying how individual neurons respond and modifying how strongly neurons influence one another. The resulting changes affect circuit dynamics, linking cellular properties and interactions within the network.

The authors argue that functional circuits should consequently be understood in relation to their modulatory environment. A description of which neurons are connected does not, by itself, capture the conductance balance and synaptic strengths under which those connections operate. The paper’s central implication is that understanding circuit function requires considering the modulatory conditions that shape both neuronal activity and communication.
neurips-1993-dynamic-modulation-of-neuro.tldr: Neuromodulators change both neuronal properties and synaptic strength, making circuit function dependent on its chemical environment.

paragraphs: Principal Components Pruning is a method for removing excess network parameters after supervised training. Its goal is both to simplify the trained network and to improve generalization, meaning performance beyond the training examples. The method examines activity within the network rather than relying only on the values of individual weights.

The procedure applies principal component analysis to node activations in successive layers. Its required information consists of the weights and node-activity correlation matrices for each layer. This makes relationships among node responses central to the pruning decision. The authors emphasize that the procedure requires neither network retraining nor calculation of the cost function’s full Hessian.

The paper demonstrates the method on regression with polynomial basis functions and on economic time-series prediction using a two-layer feed-forward network. These applications support the authors’ description of the approach as effective and inexpensive to implement. The practical contribution is a post-training simplification procedure that uses layer activity statistics while avoiding two potentially costly steps: full second-order calculation and renewed training.
neurips-1993-fast-pruning-using-principa.tldr: Principal Components Pruning removes excess network parameters using layer activation statistics without retraining or computing a full Hessian.

paragraphs: Spotting systems must detect target patterns amid many kinds of irrelevant input. Their useful performance depends on detecting targets while keeping false alarms within an acceptable range. This paper trains a network directly for that tradeoff through a figure of merit, defined by detection performance over the false-alarm range of interest.

The method computes each input pattern’s contribution to the figure-of-merit gradient and uses backpropagation to maximize the objective. This removes the need for thresholds during training. It also concentrates accurate posterior-probability modeling on patterns that materially affect detection in the relevant false-alarm range, directing network resources toward the decisions that influence the evaluation measure.

Applied to a wordspotter combining a radial basis function network with a hidden Markov model, the method increased detection accuracy by five percentage points on the credit-card speech corpus. The finding supports aligning the training objective with the operational detection criterion. Here, that alignment concerns a particular range of acceptable false alarms, rather than detection accuracy considered in isolation.
neurips-1993-figure-of-merit-training-fo.tldr: Directly optimizing detection over an acceptable false-alarm range improved a hybrid wordspotter’s accuracy by five percentage points.

paragraphs: Human genes contain short coding regions, called exons, separated by highly variable noncoding regions, called introns. This paper applies hidden Markov models to representing these regions and detecting splice sites. The problem involves understanding how different kinds of sequence regions are arranged, as well as identifying the locations where those regions meet.

The modeling task therefore brings together the internal patterns of exons and introns with their organization along a genetic sequence. Treating these as connected parts of one sequence-modeling problem makes the approach relevant to both regional characterization and boundary detection. The authors’ most notable reported observation concerns structure within exon regions.

They identify oscillatory patterns with a minimum period of approximately ten nucleotides that appear characteristic of exons. Such repetition suggests that the modeled coding regions contain a recurring sequence organization. The authors present this as a potentially biologically significant finding, while retaining uncertainty about its interpretation. The main reported outcome is therefore a candidate structural pattern revealed through the gene-modeling effort.
neurips-1993-hidden-markov-models-for-hu.tldr: Hidden Markov modeling of human genes reveals possible exon-associated oscillatory patterns with a minimum period near ten nucleotides.

paragraphs: This paper develops a computational approach to speech production grounded in physiological data. Its inverse-dynamics model maps desired articulator trajectories to electromyographic signals, which represent muscle activation. The task is to determine the activation needed to produce a movement, using an acquired forward model of the articulators’ musculoskeletal dynamics.

The inverse model incorporates constraints on activation range and on how smoothly activation changes over time. These constraints shape the muscle signals associated with a trajectory. The authors state that this model enables a faster speech motor-control scheme, with possible use in phoneme-to-speech synthesis through musculoskeletal dynamics and future application to speech recognition.

A separate forward acoustic model maps articulator trajectories to acoustic parameters. The paper improves this mapping by adding velocity and voicing information, allowing it to distinguish acoustic differences caused by changes in source characteristics. Together, the developments address both the muscular control of speech movements and the relationship between those movements and the resulting acoustic description.
neurips-1993-inverse-dynamics-of-speech-.tldr: The paper models muscle activation for speech movements and improves acoustic prediction using articulator velocity and voicing information.

paragraphs: Hybrid neural-network and hidden Markov speech recognizers represent time in two places: the Markov chain and the neural network. This paper examines the temporal behavior of recurrent networks and feed-forward multilayer perceptrons within such systems. Its practical focus is improving the input representation supplied to a multilayer perceptron.

The authors introduce local recurrent connections through an adaptive gamma filter. This adds a mechanism for learning temporal dependencies automatically, allowing the representation to incorporate information across time. The modification targets the neural-network side of the hybrid recognizer, where the form of the input influences the speech distinctions the network can learn.

Experiments use speaker-independent phone recognition on the TIMIT database. The gamma-filtered representation improves performance over the baseline multilayer perceptron, and combining the baseline and gamma-filter models also produces improvements. These findings support learning temporal structure within the input representation and show that the combined models can be useful together, even when the recognizer already includes a Markov model of time.
neurips-1993-learning-temporal-dependenc.tldr: An adaptive gamma filter learns temporal input dependencies and improves speaker-independent phone recognition in a hybrid neural-network/HMM system.

paragraphs: This paper combines visual speech information with acoustic speech recognition. Its preprocessing algorithms extract features from grayscale video, including mouth opening, tongue and teeth visibility, and descriptors of mouth shape and motion. The features are designed to be rapidly computable, useful across speakers, and relatively insensitive to lighting conditions.

The system uses separate time-delay neural networks for video and audio, then combines their responses through independent opinion pooling. This pooling method is Bayesian optimal under a conditional-independence assumption. The authors report that the assumption appears to hold for their data, making it an explicit part of the justification for the integration method.

On a speaker-independent task containing five utterances, the combined system has an error rate 25% lower than the acoustic subsystem alone. This is a relative reduction in error, showing that the visual stream adds useful recognition information in the tested setting. The work connects practical visual feature extraction with a probabilistically motivated method for combining two sources of speech evidence.
neurips-1993-lipreading-by-neural-networ.tldr: Combining video and acoustic neural networks reduced recognition error by 25% on a five-utterance speaker-independent task.

paragraphs: Optimal Brain Surgeon is a second-order method for pruning neural networks. This paper extends it to general error measures and explores an implementation that reduces computation and storage through a dominant-eigenspace decomposition. The aim is to broaden the method’s applicability while making its second-order calculations more manageable.

Simulations on nonlinear, noisy classification problems show improved generalization and favorable performance compared with Optimal Brain Damage. The authors find that the retraining steps required by Optimal Brain Damage can lead to worse generalization. They interpret this as potentially introducing noise back into the system, linking the pruning outcome to what happens after parameters are removed.

The paper also considers networks whose training was stopped at the minimum validation error. Optimal Brain Surgeon further reduced test error in that setting, while Optimal Brain Damage did not. This indicates that pruning can provide an additional benefit after validation-based stopping. The results also support the approximation used by Optimal Brain Surgeon and the concern that retraining a heavily pruned network may harm performance.
neurips-1993-optimal-brain-surgeon-exten.tldr: Extensions to Optimal Brain Surgeon improve its practicality and show generalization benefits beyond validation-based stopping in reported simulations.

paragraphs: This paper uses a convolutional neural network to locate the delivery-address block on machine-printed mail. The challenge is identifying the correct region amid unrelated printing, while handling address blocks that differ greatly in size and shape. The task concerns where the delivery information is located on the mail piece.

The locator network has four outputs, each trained to find a different corner of the address block. A simple rule set then converts the network output into candidate address locations. This divides the task into learned corner localization and rule-based construction of possible bounding regions, giving the final system several candidate answers to consider.

When allowed five guesses, the system tightly bounds the delivery-address information in 98.2% of cases. The five-guess condition is essential to interpreting this result: it measures success among a set of proposed regions. The finding shows that corner-based convolutional localization can generate highly successful address candidates despite distracting print and substantial variation in the target region’s geometry.
neurips-1993-postal-address-block-locati.tldr: A convolutional network locates address-block corners and tightly bounds delivery information in 98.2% of cases when given five guesses.

paragraphs: This paper proposes learning constraint surfaces: sets of variable combinations that can occur together. A conventional mapping assigns an output to a known input, but many vision, robotics, and control problems do not divide naturally into those roles. A surface instead represents the joint relationships that valid combinations of variables must satisfy.

The authors describe an architecture for learning and manipulating nonlinear surfaces from data. The representation supports different queries, including completion queries in which some variables are supplied and information about the remaining variables is sought. This makes the learned relationship usable with different subsets of known quantities, rather than tying every query to one fixed input-output arrangement.

The technique is demonstrated on low-dimensional synthetic surfaces and compared with nearest-neighbor approaches. It is then used to learn the space of lip images in a lipreading system intended to improve speech recognition. The learned surface improves visual tracking during recognition, showing how a model of allowable image configurations can support the tracking component of a larger recognition process.
neurips-1993-surface-learning-with-appli.tldr: Learning nonlinear constraint surfaces supports flexible queries and improves visual tracking in a lipreading application.

paragraphs: This paper studies random k-SAT formulas, where each clause contains exactly k variables and the whole formula must be satisfied simultaneously. It considers M clauses built from N variables with random negations, keeping the clause-to-variable ratio fixed. This ratio expresses how densely the formula constrains the available variables.

For k equal to two, a sharp threshold at a ratio of one was already proven: as formula size grows, instances change from almost always satisfiable to almost never satisfiable across that boundary. The authors report computer experiments for k values from two through six showing similar threshold behavior for each value.

The paper uses finite-size scaling from statistical physics to characterize how behavior near the threshold depends on formula size. Annealed and replica-based mean-field theories also give a good account of the observations. The contribution is to describe satisfiability as a collective threshold phenomenon, connecting finite computational experiments with theories of how sharp transitions emerge as systems become larger.
neurips-1993-the-statistical-mechanics-o.tldr: Experiments and statistical-physics methods characterize sharp satisfiability transitions in random k-SAT formulas.

paragraphs: This paper examines how to train neural networks when some input features are missing or uncertain. Such examples do not provide a single fully known input vector. The authors analyze how their uncertainty can be included in learning, so that incomplete examples can contribute without treating unknown values as if they had been observed.

The general solution uses weighted integration over the unknown or uncertain input. In plain terms, the training calculation accounts for possible input values with appropriate weights. This retains the distinction between an observed value and a range of plausible values. For certain Gaussian basis function networks, the authors identify less expensive closed-form solutions.

The paper also discusses situations in which replacing a missing input with its mean can be harmful. That substitution compresses uncertainty into one value, whereas the proposed general treatment carries uncertainty into the calculation itself. The contribution combines a principled formulation with computational shortcuts for particular networks, while identifying why a convenient replacement heuristic can give an unsuitable training signal.
neurips-1993-training-neural-networks-wi.tldr: Training with uncertain inputs calls for weighted integration, with efficient solutions available for certain Gaussian basis function networks.

paragraphs: This paper develops learning rules for systems that extract multiple features without supervision. The rules come from gradient ascent on explicit quality functions, meaning the learning updates seek to increase a defined measure of feature quality. The authors consider functions formed from ratios involving higher-order moments of the extracted feature values.

One resulting system learns the principal components of the correlation matrix. The paper then argues that principal components are usually not optimal features for classification. This motivates alternative quality functions intended to produce feature vectors that support unsupervised classification, making the desired use of the representation part of the objective’s design.

The authors compare the resulting systems on artificially designed datasets and a database containing all Munsell color spectra. These comparisons examine how different objectives shape the extracted features. The central contribution is a systematic route from a chosen quality measure to a learning rule, together with the distinction between recovering principal components and producing representations suited to separating classes without supervision.
neurips-1993-unsupervised-parallel-featu.tldr: Explicit statistical quality functions yield unsupervised feature-learning rules, including alternatives to principal components aimed at classification.

paragraphs: This paper investigates what could make a genetic algorithm faster than hill climbing on a simple Royal Road function. Its starting point is an earlier result in which a simple hill-climbing algorithm, RMHC, outperformed a genetic algorithm. The authors analyze that hill-climbing method to clarify the comparison rather than assuming a genetic algorithm must have the advantage.

They then analyze an idealized genetic algorithm that is significantly faster than RMHC and provides a lower bound for genetic-algorithm speed. The idealization creates a setting in which the sources of the speed advantage can be examined. The authors identify the features responsible for that advantage and discuss incorporating them into a real genetic algorithm.

The contribution is an explanation of how the relative outcome could change when a genetic algorithm has the relevant properties. The distinction between the idealized algorithm and an implementable one is central: the faster result motivates design choices for practical algorithms. It connects a disappointing comparison with an analysis of what would be needed to reverse it.
neurips-1993-when-will-a-genetic-algorit.tldr: An idealized genetic algorithm outpaces hill climbing on a Royal Road function, revealing features that could improve practical genetic algorithms.
